subtitle: A practical guide to the current editing tools: small first edits, advanced workflows, actual editing and appearance examples, a glossary and an alphabetical index.
scope: This guide covers the six supported cartridge systems. The offline catalog identifies 942 exact revisions. Recognized ROM formats can be inspected and edited as bytes without a catalog match. Game-specific editors use checked definitions.
basic_summary: Start the application, choose saved preferences, identify a source, make a focused edit, preserve progress and export a checked patch. These procedures build the habits used throughout the guide.
advanced_summary: Use checked definitions for graphics, text, tables and audio. Trace a resource to its stored bytes, compare builds and automate bounded checks.
attribution: By RetchEWretched. ROMancer code and original fixtures use the project MIT license. Instructional screenshots show third-party games, including Castlevania, Chrono Trigger, The Immortal, Final Fantasy Legend II, Deja Vu I & II and Rastan. Their imagery and trademarks remain those of their respective rights holders and are separate from the code license. No ROM files, game saves, emulator states, firmware dumps or authentication data are included. PDF and HTML work offline; PDF rebuilding optionally uses ReportLab.

chapters.title: Install, open and choose a workspace
chapters.intro: The full Windows x64 and Linux x86-64 releases include Python, Pillow and credited emulator engines. The source edition uses your own Python installation. All include this guide.
steps: On Windows, extract the entire ROMancer ZIP and double-click ROMancer.exe. Keep it beside the ROMancer Files folder.
On Linux, extract the archive and run ./ROMancer.sh. It needs glibc 2.28+ and a web browser.

For the source edition, install Python 3.13 or 3.14 and the pinned requirements, then use Launch ROMancer.cmd on Windows or the supplied run.sh launcher. Read the root README for the command-line and MCP entry points.
Open Help for this guide. Start a workshop or import a ROM you supply. No AI account, subscription or API key is required.
chapters.result: ROMancer opens its local interface and your project list. The full Windows and Linux editions select a matching included engine when you load a supported system.
chapters.note: Keep the portable folder intact. Projects are stored separately. Game-specific editors use checked definitions for the selected revision.

details.title: Update and recovery
details.text: Extract the new release into its own folder and start it from there. Projects stay in the separate workspace, so the new copy opens them. Keep the earlier folder as your rollback. Older applications may have limited support for newer project features.

Each requires its matching original ROM. Advanced users and AI clients can use the same review and build operations through the local API or MCP.

chapters.title: Original, draft, build and patch: what changes?
chapters.kicker: Five useful terms / read this first
chapters.intro: The editor, playable game and shared patch are different things. This is how to tell what you have saved and what you are testing.
steps: Original ROM: the starting game file. Importing keeps a project copy. Editing creates separate outputs and preserves this original.

Draft: your saved editor changes. Draft saved means they can be reopened. Edits not built means they are not in a playable output yet. Undo and Redo change this draft; they do not erase an older build.
Build: a separate ROM made from reviewed changes. Create a build after editing. Playtest saved build selects that output; newer draft changes need another build.

Patch: a small file containing your changes for sharing. Export saved build selects the original and edited build. Create verified patch checks reconstruction. The recipient supplies the matching original ROM.

Game save versus save state: a game save holds normal progress, often in a .sav file. A save state is a snapshot of the whole emulator session and belongs to one exact ROM/build and emulator setup. Use Save state and Load state to return to that moment.
chapters.result: Before Play or Export, check the selected file at the top. A saved draft and a saved build are different: only the build contains your new playable ROM edits.
chapters.note: You do not need to learn hex, addresses or codecs to try the included original studio. Editing an unfamiliar game may require research and a verified editing setup.

chapters.title: Set preferences and choose a theme
chapters.intro: Settings control the working environment: appearance, startup behavior, automatic analysis and audio defaults. Apply the choices you want to keep before closing the application.
steps: Open Settings. Review appearance and startup preferences. 100% is the standard interface size; it uses the more compact layout previously shown at 75%. Choose another offered size when useful.

Choose ROMancer (default) for the original ROMancer teal palette and deeper menu/input surfaces; Dark for graphite or Light for grey panels on a light background. Keep Advanced tools expanded controls the navigation group.

Review Auto deep scan on ROM load, enabled by default, and Inspect gameplay graphics automatically. Set Remember my workspace to reopen the last project, ROM, page and editing position. These preferences choose automatic work, not a new level of game-format verification.

Set Volume from 0 to 100, Start game audio muted and Loop audio previews. Choose Apply to save and continue, or OK to save and close. Cancel discards unapplied changes. Restore defaults prepares the standard choices; use Apply or OK to keep that reset.
chapters.result: Applied preferences persist across launches for this workspace. The chosen theme and size make the controls comfortable to read, and automatic scan/audio behavior follows the saved choices.
chapters.note: Basic editing pages stay visible. Expand Advanced for Game view, Resources, Investigation, Recipes & definitions, Routes and Regression. Deeper menu/input surfaces and a visible focus outline distinguish controls. Theme changes do not change game palettes.

details.title: When to change automatic work
details.text: Leave Auto deep scan on ROM load enabled for normal discovery. Turn it off when you want to choose the timing of a manual scan. Automatic analysis of paused gameplay graphics depends on an actual loaded session and exposed data; it does not identify arbitrary resource ownership.

details.title: Audio and motion
details.text: Volume and start-muted preferences control playback defaults; use the current preview controls when listening. Preview looping repeats the available preview, not the game sequence. Reduce interface motion makes movement in the interface less distracting.

details.title: Apply, Cancel and defaults
details.text: Apply saves the currently selected preferences without closing Settings. Cancel does not roll back an earlier Apply. Restore defaults prepares the standard choices for review; use Apply or OK to keep them.

Levels is listed as coming soon and is disabled in this release. Expand Advanced for Game view, Resources/hex, Investigation, Recipes & definitions, Routes and Regression. A direct task opens the matching group automatically.

chapters.title: Understand test results and report a problem
chapters.intro: A passing automated check describes the exact scenario it ran. It does not mean every ROM, edit or computer configuration is certified.
steps: Read README.txt for what was checked in this release and what was only measured. A skipped test is not a pass.

If a file cannot import, read the exact error. An HTML page saved as .7z is not an archive; obtain your real cartridge file and extract a valid archive before importing. Never rename an error page to .sms.
Open Settings, expand Diagnostics & support, run checks and prepare a support report. Review it before sharing; exclude ROMs, saves, states, private backups, credentials and personal paths.
For a bug report, record version/build, operating system, scale setting, exact steps, expected result and actual result. Prefer reproducing with an included workshop.
Use the bug report form on the GitHub repository. Report security problems privately to the repository maintainer; do not post secrets publicly.
chapters.result: A short, reproducible report gives another person enough information to investigate without your commercial game data.
chapters.note: Automated accessibility/contrast checks and keyboard navigation help find problems. They do not replace a human screen-reader trial, an independent beginner trial or testing Windows-wide display scaling on a clean machine.

details.title: Known formats and reviewed engines
details.text: Import accepts recognized supported cartridge layouts. Unknown, ambiguous or unsupported layouts are blocked. The full Windows runtime checks emulator binaries against the included open-source pins before native loading. A known console header does not identify every game resource; unavailable sound or compression interpretations cannot be treated as editable definitions.

details.title: Useful byte explanations
details.text: After opening a known or declared graphics resource, use Resources -> Explain selected bytes. The report identifies the stored tile/cell, row and bitplane or packed-pixel ordering, and declared palette channel values. It does not invent an enemy name or behavior for undeclared bytes.

chapters.title: Start with a project
steps: Click New project. Give this piece of work a useful name, then import your ROM into that project.

Check the ROM or build selected at the top. On Overview, read What can I edit in this ROM?. Choose Edit graphics, Edit text, Edit stats or Edit sound when ready. Follow a setup action when a checked layout is needed. Choose Inspect ROM bytes for offsets, search and comparisons.
Make one small edit, review it, create a separate build, then playtest that build. Export its patch after checking the result.
chapters.result: A project holds owned source copies, editing setup, builds and evidence. Start a new project for unrelated work.
chapters.note: The Windows x64 and Linux x86-64 packages include their runtime and emulator engines. Supply your own ROMs. GB and GBC use separate system modes.
chapters.intro: A project keeps one piece of work together: original ROMs, saved editing changes, playable builds and test results. Start with the included editing studio to practice, or import your own ROM.
chapters.caption: Current Basic workspace and per-ROM readiness. Common editors stay visible; Game view, Resources and engineering tools are under Advanced.

details.title: Choose an editing tool

details.title: Basic first, Advanced when needed
details.text: Text, graphics, stats, music, playtesting and export stay in the main navigation. Open Advanced for Game view, Resources, native investigation, reusable definitions, routes or regression checks. The offline guide has Basic and Advanced sections.

chapters.title: Practice real edits in Mossy Hollow
chapters.kicker: Original playable example / normal editing tools
chapters.intro: Choose Try the editing studio to open the original NES practice game. Use its graphics, text, numbers and music layouts, then run the build in Playtest.
steps: Graphics: open Graphics & fonts, set Tiles across and Tiles down to 2, then Assemble tiles. Paint the first four hero tiles, try Undo and Redo, review and create a separate graphics build. Edit the second hero animation too for a consistent result.
Dialogue: select the Original again and open Text & layout. Replace HELLO, EXPLORER! with WELCOME, ROM HACKER! Check capacity, review and build. The character table supports uppercase letters.
Movement: choose Edit stats on Overview. Change Hero speed from 2 to 3, review and build. Compare equal Right input frames in Playtest. Zero stops movement; the checked limit is 8 pixels per frame.

Music: in Music & sound, click a melody note or choose its Event, change Note number and choose Stage note edit. Inspect the note view and Original/Edited waveform previews. Review, build and listen in Playtest.

Playtest controls: arrows move, A attacks an overlapping enemy and chirps, Start restarts. HP 0 stops the hero; an enemy with 0 health disappears. Save/load states belong to that exact build. Export and verify a patch from its Original.
chapters.result: Review your edits, save a separate build, playtest it and verify its patch export.
chapters.note: Mossy Hollow is an original practice game. Use Playtest for the live scene.

chapters.title: Your first complete edit: the original NES workshop
chapters.intro: Use the included original drawing program to learn the full workflow without finding offsets or supplying a commercial game.
steps: Save existing work and return to the empty Overview. Expand More practice ROMs, then click NES workshop.
Open Graphics & fonts. Keep First tile 0, Tiles across 1 and Tiles down 1; click Assemble tiles. Leave Preview size on Fit and click brush swatch 1.
Focus the Editing canvas. Press Right Arrow once, then Space. Expect 1 pixel differs. Choose Undo sprite stroke to restore the pixel and Redo sprite stroke to stage the change again.

Choose Load game, then Play. Pause to inspect the result. The full Windows and Linux editions supply the engine; the source edition may require core setup.

details.title: What a review summary counts
details.text: Counts come from exact before/after bytes, with overlapping ranges merged. Listed checksum/header updates are included. Large or unfamiliar reports retain their technical detail instead of an invented count. No game-specific meaning is inferred from a changed byte.

chapters.title: Complete the beginner acceptance checklist
chapters.intro: Ask someone unfamiliar with ROMancer to follow this guide alone. Use the unmarked user-guide/ACCEPTANCE.txt record. The automated agent exercise is separate; the independent human trial has not been completed.
steps: Open the app and choose Try the editing studio. Open Graphics & fonts, assemble its first four tiles as a 2 by 2 image and make one visible pixel change. Confirm that Original stays unchanged.

Undo and redo the stroke. Review and name a separate build. Choose Playtest saved build, load it, advance to the edited scene, then save and load a state. Export saved build must select that output and its correct original; create and verify the patch.
Play and pause the build. Save and load a matching state, then export and download a verified BPS patch. Identify the original, build and patch as separate files.

Close and reopen the project, then find the same source and build. On the original, stage one more edit, wait for Saved and reload. If a confirmation appears, continue only after saving. Confirm the draft and its staged-change status return.

Read the labels and previews at your preferred window size and theme. Mark a box in your checklist copy complete only when you can explain the result without outside help. Skipped or confusing steps stay unchecked.
chapters.result: Every copied checklist checkbox is completed by the person doing the trial. For a problem, record the step, expected result, observed result, application build and any unclear label. Screenshots help reproduce visual problems.
chapters.note: A saved editing draft still needs a new reviewed build before it affects gameplay. Automated checks and the walkthrough video are separate evidence; they do not fill in the human-trial boxes.

details.title: What counts as a usability issue
details.text: Needing someone to find a button, confusing a draft with a build, losing track of the selected file, unreadable labels or an unclear recovery prompt all count, even if the underlying operation eventually succeeds.

details.title: Record a useful report
details.text: Describe what you clicked and what you expected. Attach a screenshot or a sanitized support report if useful. Keep ROM data, private paths and personal saves out of a public report.

chapters.title: Identify the ROM and its exact revision
chapters.intro: A system header, an exact hash match and a successful playtest answer different questions. Read each result before selecting a named game edit.
steps: Select the imported source and open Resources. Read ROM health & revision and the investigation summary. A filename is a hint, not a verified identity.
For a known reference, use Identify ROM revision. Import your offline CSV, TSV, JSON or XML DAT catalog and select whole-file or supported cartridge-payload scope.
Compare CRC32, SHA-1 or SHA-256 with an expected value for that same scope. Check the region, revision and any copier/header prefix. A mismatch is against the selected reference.
Use Check project on Overview for missing files, stale definitions, overlaps and declared pointer/allocation problems. Recheck after repairing the reported location.
chapters.result: A catalog match identifies exact referenced bytes. Unknown means no matching reference was established. It does not prove corruption. A project check reports its declared structural checks.
chapters.note: A valid console checksum does not prove every game-specific check passes. Hashes do not prove that an edit is fun, balanced or safe in every scene.

details.title: Three separate checks
details.text: Identity: compare measured bytes with an expected revision. Structure: validate supported headers, declared sizes and integrity fields. Behavior: playtest and replay explicit assertions. Keep these conclusions separate.

details.title: Headers and byte scope
details.text: A SNES copier prefix or an NES trainer/header can change file positions and whole-file hashes. Compare a payload reference only with the matching supported payload scope. Never force a named definition onto a close-looking revision.

chapters.caption: Expected 00000000 was entered solely to demonstrate this warning. Compare the measured CRC with a trusted reference for the same byte scope; do not replace it with a convenient value just to clear the warning.

chapters.title: Use the offline ROM facts database
chapters.intro: The offline catalog recognizes all 942 supplied cartridge revisions. Exact SHA-256 and file size select a record. CRC32 and SHA-1 can help cross-check your copy.
steps: Import your ROM. In Overview, expand Playtest audit to see the Windows engine's observations for that exact file. Seven previously refused revisions now show a verified title and opening gameplay. Test changes to your own build in Playtest.

In Overview, use What can I edit in this ROM? to open an available named edit. For file details, open Advanced > Resources, then ROM investigation. Expand Measured file facts & locations or Related source evidence.
Choose Inspect bytes to open a location in the selected source. Confirm its role with a checked definition or native investigation before planning an edit.
Review the preview, create a build, then use Check my hack and Export saved build in the footer. Your build has a new file hash and needs a fresh playtest.
chapters.result: You can begin with measured addresses and format facts while keeping candidates, trusted game meanings and actual gameplay observations separate.
chapters.note: Each supplied ROM was read in full. Header fields and checks describe the exact file. Sampled graphics, possible text and bounded compression results retain their evidence labels.

details.title: What is recorded
details.text: The facts catalog stores hashes, sizes, header numbers, numeric checks and bounded candidate ranges. The separate source-evidence index records 3,648 directly measured relationships; 554 files have at least one. Reference associations cover 905 files. NES comparisons match PRG/CHR input inventories and exclude the container header. Entire-file comparisons on other systems describe named ROM inputs, not complete gameplay validity.

details.title: Maintenance and automation · Advanced
details.text: AI clients can query rom.evidence with sha256 and size without creating a project or loading a ROM. Results show at most eight relationships and eight exact BRR segment locations, plus total counts. rom.scan.run exposes source_evidence and recorded_facts; altered builds need their own investigation. Sound-context matches and driver-pattern candidates do not supply sequence formats, pointers, ownership or editing permissions.

details.title: Redistribution basis
details.text: The packaged indexes contain measured facts, reference identifiers and hashes of private verification receipts. No game code, decoded images, sound payloads, save states or personal paths are included. Reference inventory matches do not authorize redistribution of source games or separate chip firmware. Nintendo and other marks remain their owners’ property.

chapters.title: Save drafts, undo and create a build
chapters.intro: Editing changes the proposal shown in the editor. A build is a separate playable output created from a reviewed plan.
steps: Watch the Saving or Saved status as you work. Ctrl+S requests draft saving. A saved draft still needs review and a build.
Use the active editor's Undo and Redo controls. Pixel editing groups a stroke; text fields retain ordinary text editing undo. The shortcut help explains the current context.
Choose Review changes or the tool's equivalent. Read expected original bytes, proposed values, shared consumers and any integrity updates. Changing an input invalidates an older review.

Create the separate build. Playtest saved build in the bottom bar selects that output and opens Playtest; choose Load game. Export saved build selects that output and its ancestral original. A newer staged edit needs a new build.
chapters.result: The source remains intact, the build has its own identity, and the selected Playtest file is the output you just created.
chapters.note: If saving fails, keep the window open and copy unsaved text before reloading. Undoing staged work does not erase a previously created build.

details.title: Draft versus plan
details.text: Drafts hold editor values and staged changes. A plan binds exact changes and preconditions to a source identity. Re-review when the source, definition or staged values change.

details.title: Returning to earlier work
details.text: Saved-build controls derive from the recorded project history and survive closing and reopening the app. They follow the selected build, or the latest direct build of the selected input; another ROM branch is excluded. Edit input restores that build's immediate input and saved editor. Navigating between Playtest and Export preserves a paused session when the selected build stays the same. A restart requires loading the game and its saved state again.

details.title: Name the output before creating it
details.text: Open Name and notes for this build (optional), enter up to 120 name characters and 2000 note characters, then create the reviewed build. Notes can span lines. Names and notes are metadata; they do not alter the output bytes. Existing builds remain editable through Build history.

chapters.title: Keep discoveries with the exact ROM
chapters.intro: A useful discovery should be easy to find again. Research notes name a byte range and record what you observed without turning a theory into a verified game format.
steps: Open Resources and use Resource browser & research to search saved graphics, text, numbers, sound or notes. Bytes opens the exact range; Editor opens the saved layout.
Expand Research note. Choose New note at selected byte, enter a short name, file offset and byte length, then record what you found and its evidence reference.
Choose Save note. The note belongs to this exact source revision and does not change the ROM. Select Edit note to load its complete text, or Remove to delete it after confirmation.
In the hex editor, choose Explain selected bytes. Matching notes appear under User research, separately from decoded storage facts.

If opening an editor would replace a different setup draft, choose Keep current draft or Load saved setup. Loading first stores a recovery copy; Resources > Previous editor setups can restore it. Document-specific pixel and text edits remain separate.

chapters.title: Turn understood bytes into a named editor
chapters.intro: Once you have located data and checked its storage layout, a form can turn it into a useful editor. You do not need to write JSON for ordinary numeric tables, tile graphics or ASCII text slots.
steps: In Resources, inspect the relevant file bytes. Expand Build an editor from these bytes, choose Numbers & stats, Graphics tiles or Text slots, then choose the type.

For numbers, enter the first file offset, record count and bytes per record. Name each field, give its byte position within a record, and choose its stored number type and byte order. Update fields when changing the field count.
Choose Preview editor. Check the decoded values, tiles or text against your evidence. A regular-looking result is not proof that you found health, enemies or dialogue.

Choose Save & open editor. If a current definition would be replaced, acknowledge it first. If another window or operation changed the source research, preview again. Existing editor setup drafts may require their separate recovery choice.
Use the opened editor to stage changes, undo or redo them, review, create a separate build, playtest and export a verified patch. Saving a layout alone does not modify the ROM.
chapters.result: A reusable exact-source definition opens in the appropriate editing tool, with the same decoded fields that you reviewed.
chapters.note: In the current original Mossy Hollow studio, actor health and contact damage begin at file offset 0x1D16, with two records 16 bytes apart. Fields at byte 0 and 1 decode Health 5/3 and Contact damage 1/1. This is a workshop-specific example; do not transfer these offsets to another ROM. Health for that runtime stays 1–9.

Create the build and playtest the actual menu. Use Text & layout for declared script records and translation imports.
chapters.result: The preview shows both strings; the review also names the guarded game-specific adjustment required by this definition.
chapters.note: The preview uses the system font. The real game font and window still need playtesting. This named definition preserves its protected terminator; do not copy its offsets to another revision.

chapters.title: Change a color and see every scene it touches
chapters.kicker: SCENES AND COLORS / NEW IN v1.1
chapters.intro: A color in a game is usually shared. The same few bytes can paint a title screen, a menu and a level. Scenes & colors lets you change a color, redraw a picture or repaint the background, and look at every recorded moment of the game that changes with it, before anything is saved. It works with NES, Super NES, Mega Drive, Master System, Game Boy and Game Boy Color games, and needs no game-specific definition.
steps: Select your ROM in the top bar and open Scenes & colors. A scene is a moment of the game that ROMancer has watched. To collect scenes, choose Record more scenes and the game plays by itself for a few minutes, or choose Play and capture a moment, play to the screen you want and choose Capture this moment. Stop recording ends a recording early.

Choose a scene. Click a pixel in its picture, or choose a swatch under Colors in this scene. Pick the new color. The controls offer only colors the console can show: sliders on most systems, the console color chart on NES, and four shades on the original Game Boy.

Under Where should it change?, keep Everywhere this color is used, or choose Only in this scene when it is offered. Only in this scene gives that scene its own copy of the color data. ROMancer then checks by replay that the other scenes stay as they are.

Choose Show what changes. The Also changes strip fills with every recorded scene that uses the same data. Each picture is the real game replayed with your change, not a guess. Scenes marked Looks different come first. Choose a picture to compare before and after.
Choose Keep this change to add it to the Change list, or Cancel to drop it. Nothing is written yet. In the list, Show scenes brings the pictures back and Undo removes the change.

Choose Review and save. ROMancer replays every affected scene with all your changes together and lists everything that changes. Save as a new build writes a separate playable copy, then offers Playtest saved build and Download patch.
chapters.result: The new build carries your colors, and the cartridge checksum is updated when the game has one. Your original ROM is unchanged. You saw every recorded scene that changed before you saved.
chapters.note: Used in N scenes counts only the scenes you have recorded. Scenes you haven't recorded can't be shown. Before you save, record the places you care about, and playtest the build afterwards.

details.title: What "Used in N scenes" means
details.text: ROMancer learns where a color is used by watching the game run. The count beside a color, and the pictures in the Also changes strip, cover the scenes recorded so far and nothing else. A color used in 3 recorded scenes may also be used in a level you have not reached. Recording more of the game makes the answer more complete; it never makes it guaranteed. A scene can also use the changed data without showing it at that moment. Those are listed as Uses changed data; nothing visible at this moment.

details.title: Locked colors
details.text: A swatch with a lock cannot be changed here. Choose it to see why. There are two reasons. The game may work the color out while it runs, as in a fade or a blend, so there is no single stored color to change. Or ROMancer has not seen where the color comes from: it was set before recording started, or the slot is unused. A scene recorded at a different moment often shows the same color unlocked.

details.title: When a change is not confirmed
details.text: After you choose Show what changes, the real engine replays the scene with the edited bytes. If the color on screen does not become the one you picked, the editor says so, and the change is marked Not confirmed by replay in the Change list. Undo it unless you have a reason to keep it.

details.title: Where scenes are kept
details.text: Scenes, their replay savestates and the Change list are stored inside the project and are included in a complete private project backup. They belong to the original ROM. To make another version, keep editing the original and save again. Forget this scene removes one scene.

details.title: If the tracing engine is not installed
details.text: Scenes & colors uses a second, tracing build of each emulator engine, kept in the trace-cores folder beside the app. The full Windows and Linux packages include it. A copy without that folder shows a message naming the system instead of the editor. Scenes & colors is not available for Kirby Tilt ’n’ Tumble, because its tracing engine is not included. Playtest is not affected.

chapters.image_alt: Scenes & colors in Graphics mode: one 8 by 8 picture opened from the scene and redrawn, with the scenes that use it listed below
chapters.caption: Graphics mode. Click a pixel in the scene to open the picture under it, redraw it, then choose Show what changes.
chapters.title: Redraw a picture or repaint the background
chapters.kicker: SCENES AND COLORS / NEW IN v1.1
chapters.intro: Scenes & colors also edits what the game draws with. Graphics redraws one of the small pictures a scene is built from. Background changes which picture each cell of a background layer shows. As with colors, every recorded scene that uses the same data is replayed before anything is saved.
steps: Open Scenes & colors, choose a scene and choose Graphics above it. Click a picture in the scene, or choose it from the list.
Redraw the picture pixel by pixel with the colors of its palette. You can also save it as an 8 by 8 PNG, edit it in any drawing program and load it back.
To change the background instead, choose Background. Choose the picture to paint with, then paint it into the cells of the layer.
Choose Show what changes and read the Also changes strip, then Keep this change. Review and save writes a separate build, as it does for colors.
chapters.result: The new build shows your picture or background. Your original ROM is unchanged.
chapters.note: A locked picture or cell cannot be changed here. The game builds it while it runs, or ROMancer has not seen where it comes from. A scene recorded at another moment may show it unlocked.

details.title: Packed pictures and the run-time patch
details.text: Many games keep their pictures packed to save space. When ROMancer recognises the packing, it unpacks the data, applies your change and packs it again. When it does not, the saved build gets a small run-time patch that swaps your picture in as the game loads it. The editor then shows two results: the scene itself, and the game started from power-on. Read both before you keep the change.

details.title: What to expect
details.text: Measured across the catalog on development builds of the tracing engines, a color edit was confirmed by replay on 906 of 938 ROMs and a picture edit on 916 of 938. Only in this scene is rarely available; expect a change to apply everywhere the data is used. Super NES replays are slow: with many recorded scenes, Show what changes and Review and save can take minutes.

chapters.title: Playtest, pause and save a state
steps: Check that the top selector shows the source or build you intend to test, then open Playtest and click Load game.
Choose Play and focus the game for controller input. Pause on a useful scene. Use Inspect graphics, Track a value, or Save comparison scene.
Choose Save state. Select a saved state and click Load state to return to it. Ordinary battery saves are managed separately below.
chapters.result: The screenshot shows a paused session of the included Mossy Hollow practice game. For the verified Kirby Tilt ’n’ Tumble revision, confirm calibration with the game’s A button, then hold a direction to tilt and release it to return to neutral.
chapters.note: Save states are bound to the exact ROM, engine and runtime setup. Do not assume a state from the original will load on a modified build. Loading refreshes one paused frame. Unload game closes only the current emulator session. Builds, saved states and ordinary game saves remain in the project.
chapters.intro: Choose the ROM or build to test. Load game selects the bundled engine and the settings for a recognized cartridge. Play starts the session.
chapters.caption: Mossy Hollow paused in Playtest after a save state was loaded.

details.title: Top Gear 3000 save states
details.text: Load the verified cartridge with Load game and create a new state. ROMancer v1.0.0 and later save the DSP-4 chip state needed to resume the race. States made with the older engine lack that data and cannot be repaired. Verify by reloading a new state and repeating an input from the same point.

chapters.title: Keep battery saves and states separate
chapters.intro: A battery save is persistent game data such as raw .sav or .srm RAM. A save state captures an emulator session and has much tighter compatibility requirements.
steps: For a snapshot, use Save state beside Play. Select the timestamped state for the same ROM, core and setup, then use Load state. Loading refreshes one paused frame.
For ordinary progress, load the exact game and open Battery saves. Back up the currently exposed save RAM before importing or restarting.
Import raw save data only at the exact supported size. Keep a downloaded backup. Use the game's own load/save menu to confirm progress after a restart.
Use Restart with selected save only after reviewing the chosen file and automatic backup. Keep separate progress for experiments until the edited build is validated.
chapters.result: The selected data has the expected size and identity, a backup exists, and the game can load the intended progress through its normal save system.
chapters.note: A state from an original can be incompatible with a modified build. Wrapped emulator saves are not automatically raw RAM; use the originating emulator's export tools.

details.title: Binding matters
details.text: States depend on exact ROM bytes, engine build, options and system-file setup. Do not treat a matching game title as compatibility. Battery files can also depend on the game revision and save layout.

details.title: Size or initialization mismatch
details.text: Some games expose a different save size after initialization. A refusal preserves the backup; do not pad, truncate or bypass exact-size checks without a separately understood format.

chapters.title: Export a verified patch
steps: Open Export. Select the exact Original ROM and the intended Edited build. Add a useful title and notes.
Click Create verified patch. ROMancer reconstructs the target with a separate BPS decoder and checks its identity.
Download the prepared patch. Include the expected original revision and instructions with your release, then test applying that patch to a fresh source copy.
chapters.result: The capture follows a successful patch preparation from the modified Chrono Trigger build.
chapters.note: A patch is not a full ROM. BPS checks compatibility using embedded checksums; IPS needs an external source reference. A verified patch proves reconstruction, not complete gameplay correctness. To apply a downloaded patch, use Export > Apply a downloaded patch on the exact original. BPS carries checksums; IPS requires the author's full-file CRC32 or SHA-256 reference. Preview compatibility before creating its separate build.
chapters.intro: Share the verified difference between an exact original and a completed build. State the required source revision with your instructions.
chapters.caption: Actual ROMancer interface. The HTML edition links to the full-resolution capture.

chapters.title: Save a discovery and share a replay proof
chapters.intro: A discovery saves an editable layout for the exact original. A replay proof lets a recipient rebuild your patch and rerun the same checks on their own original.
steps: After an original-to-build replay passes, expand Save a reusable discovery. Give a changed byte, saved table or saved graphics resource a clear name. Numeric discoveries require passing gameplay expectations.

Select the original again. Open Overview and expand Saved discoveries. Open the editor or choose Prepare JSON export. Find the file under Export. Import discoveries on the exact matching ROM. To mark an imported discovery as locally checked, reproduce its replay and save the same discovery again.
In Export, select the original and build used in the check. Under Share a patch with replay proof, pick the completed replay and create the ZIP. Screenshots are optional.

On the receiving copy, extract the ZIP and apply Patch.bps to the exact original. Select the original and patched build in Export, then load Patch.bps and Replay.json under Verify a shared replay. Choose Run shared replay.
chapters.result: ROMancer verifies the BPS output, repeats the two original runs and one build run, and compares the frames and any saved gameplay measurements using the recorded engine settings.
chapters.note: The ZIP includes the patch, written instructions and replay data. Leave screenshots unchecked when you only intend to share those files. If verification rejects the package, compare the original hash, patched hash and engine settings in the README.
chapters.caption: A saved Mossy Hollow discovery reopened on the original ROM.

chapters.title: Apply a downloaded BPS or IPS patch safely
chapters.kicker: Exact source / compatibility preview / separate build
chapters.intro: A patch requires an exact source revision. ROMancer-v1.0.0-Hack-Examples.zip, inside the Extras ZIP on the GitHub release, includes three BPS examples. Its README lists each change and the matching original hash.
steps: On Export, expand Apply a patch downloaded from someone else. Choose the exact ROM the patch requires in the top bar, then select or drop its BPS or IPS patch.

Under Apply a downloaded patch, choose or drop one BPS or IPS file. For IPS, enter the author's full-file reference: eight hexadecimal CRC32 digits or 64 SHA-256 digits. BPS checks embedded checksums.
Choose Preview patch. Read the format, target size and changed-byte count. Expand Changed ranges and identities for source/target hashes and offsets. A zero-change result has nothing to build.
If the reference mismatches, stop and find the required original. Do not remove a header, edit a checksum, or substitute another revision merely to bypass the failure.
Give the output a useful name and choose Create patched build. ROMancer selects the separate output and opens Playtest. Load the game, verify the intended change, and preserve the original.
chapters.result: The pictured BPS was exported from the first-edit exercise. Preview found one changed byte; the 292-byte patch recreated exactly the same SHA-256 as the native-tested asset build.
chapters.note: Changing the selected file can restore its previous editor. Select the original first, then open Export. A valid patch reconstruction establishes bytes, not whole-game behavior. Chain patches only when the next patch explicitly requires the previous output. Patch size includes metadata; sparse runs and dense edits can encode differently. Export does not promise the smallest possible patch.

chapters.title: Check a ROM hack before sharing it
chapters.intro: Use this checklist for the output you intend to distribute. Keep tested observations separate from unknown behavior.
steps: On Overview, run Check project. Resolve errors, read warnings and verify the selected original/build identities. A validation pass covers declared formats, not every gameplay path.
Reload the final build in Playtest. Test the intended change and one nearby behavior that should remain unchanged. Check input and any relevant save/load behavior on this exact build.
For repeatable checks, record routes and screenshot regions. Read Original, Build and Difference results. State which routes and conditions were actually tested.

In Export, create and independently verify the final patch. Confirm the required original revision and full-file hash. Apply the downloaded patch to an unchanged source and compare the reconstructed target hash.

Review Release selection before packaging exports. Only approved patch/document roles enter that package. Keep private project backups, ROM images, saves, captures and personal reports out of the shared selection.

Keep a complete private backup and write clear instructions: required original, patch order if any, expected target identity, intended changes and known limits. Perform a final hands-on trial before announcing success.
chapters.result: A reproducible patch and instructions linked to the exact tested build, with a recovery copy kept separately.
chapters.note: Passing a route or reconstruction check does not certify an entire game. For ROMancer itself, automated release checks are recorded separately; independent human usability feedback still requires a person.

chapters.title: Back up, restore and recover a project
chapters.intro: A project backup is for your own recovery or migration. A public patch package has a different purpose and contains a different selection of data.
steps: Open Projects to choose the right project before editing. Use a separate project for unrelated games or experiments you want to manage independently.
In Settings, make a complete private project backup before moving a workspace or making broad changes. Store the archive outside the working project and confirm it was created.
Restore into the destination workspace, open the recovered project and run Check project. Inspect sources, builds, definitions, drafts and prepared exports.
To remove an unwanted project from the active list, choose Delete project, then Move to Trash. Recover it through Projects > Trash > Restore.
chapters.result: A restored project opens with its owned source and build data. Deleting a project moves its owned files to Trash; the original external ROM stays where it was.
chapters.note: A private backup can contain your ROMs, saves and personal work. Review what you share. Recovery does not make historical reports into fresh native evidence.

details.title: Before cleanup
details.text: Check the project name and current workspace. Keep an independent backup before deleting old application folders or moving manually managed data. A reversible application rollback is not a project backup.

details.title: After restore
details.text: Run fresh native checks before using restored captures or reports as current proof. If a lock blocks recovery, establish that the previous owner process is no longer running; never break an active writer's lock.

chapters.title: Load a mod and compare the changed bytes
chapters.intro: Compare two files in the same project. A patch can create a separate modified build, while a supplied modded ROM can be imported as another source.
steps: Import your original ROM into a project. For a modded ROM file, use Import source in that same project. For BPS/IPS, select the original and open Export > Apply a downloaded patch. IPS requires the author’s original CRC32 or SHA-256 reference.

Choose Preview patch, inspect the changed-byte count and source identity, then Create patched build. The original remains unchanged. A successful BPS reconstruction does not establish each changed byte’s gameplay meaning.

Open Overview > Build history > Compare files. Choose the original/earlier file and the modified/later file, then click Compare files. Read the full changed-byte count and select a listed changed range.

In Resources, compare Earlier bytes and Selected bytes. Highlights mark differences. A dash means that file has no byte at that offset. Use the comparison page controls for added/removed regions, or Follow hex editor to use its current position.
chapters.result: Both columns describe the exact selected file pair at the displayed offset. The example applies a Castlevania BPS patch and compares its two changed starting-life constants.
chapters.note: A shifted or recompressed resource can change many bytes without creating many separate gameplay changes. The range list can be truncated; its changed-byte total still covers the complete comparison. File-relative differences do not prove that offsets mean the same thing after relocation.

chapters.title: Investigate a changing value without a game profile
chapters.intro: ROMancer can gather evidence from an unfamiliar ROM. Start with one number or a controlled change rather than guessing a game property from byte values.
steps: Load the selected ROM in Playtest, pause, and choose Track a value. Name what you want to change. Enter the number you see, or leave it blank to track change only.
Choose Capture before. Perform one controlled action, pause, mark what happened, and choose Capture after. Choose Open investigation to see the matches.
Add an unchanged control while unrelated activity continues. This helps reject background counters. Keep before, changed and control observations together.
Compare surviving RAM offsets, widths, byte order, signed/BCD encoding and display relationships. Additional observations help separate equally fitting hypotheses.
Choose Investigate accesses for a promising RAM result. If the inputs were recorded from power on, Replay last Playtest change repeats that route in the native debugger.
chapters.result: A source-bound observation history and tested numeric hypotheses, without a game-specific profile or a memory write.
chapters.note: Each observation covers at most 4096 bytes; an experiment keeps at most 32 observations. A new worker, reset or loaded state requires a fresh series. Restored project evidence remains historical and cannot supply fresh native proof.

chapters.intro: Game view connects saved graphics, palettes, text, named records, sound, research notes and measured gameplay across all six systems.
steps: Choose a source or build in the top bar, then open Game view. Search a resource by name or filter to graphics, named records or gameplay traces.
Select an entry. Read its preview and byte range. The confidence label tells you whether the entry comes from a checked definition, your notes or a measured frame.

Choose Open editor where available, or Inspect exact bytes to open the file location. Keep current draft preserves your work when another setup is offered.

chapters.title: Trace a captured object to candidate ROM graphics
chapters.intro: Save a real native frame region and search the selected ROM using its tested literal tile codec. Traces retain the frame, crop, searched range and every returned pixel candidate.
steps: Load the selected game in Playtest. Play or advance to the scene, pause, and choose Inspect graphics. Capture a fresh frame if needed.
In Frame region & screenshot checkpoints, drag a tight rectangle around the object, at least 8 by 8 and at most 256 by 256 pixels. Smaller regions reduce competing matches.
Under Trace gameplay to ROM data, name the trace and choose its source search range. Choose Trace selected object. Each request searches at most 512 KiB; read the reported coverage.
Review matching parts and competing source offsets. Choose Open saved trace in Game view to revisit the crop and its candidates. Search next ROM range continues an incomplete search.
Choose a confirmed candidate or explicitly select matching parts to open the graphics editor. Review the assembled result before editing, build separately, then playtest the changed scene.
chapters.result: A persistent connection from measured screen pixels to literal ROM byte candidates, available to people and the MCP interface.
chapters.note: Pixel agreement does not prove a CPU/VDP source transfer, animation ownership or the role of a sprite. Compressed, transformed or RAM-generated images can have no literal match. The supplied six-game test includes genuine zero-match and partial results; it does not claim every sprite was found. Use Verify ROM sources to test causal origins with coded probes and independent validation.

chapters.title: Check each build automatically
chapters.intro: Compare a separate build with two fresh runs of its original using identical inputs and a reviewed emulator core. A saved test can run after each descendant build or imported patch.
steps: After creating a build, choose Check my hack in the footer. The review pairs the build with its exact original. Choose Compare original and build to see changed bytes and open a range in hex.
Use Run checks to replay the configured inputs. Original, build and difference frames show the selected checkpoint. A named edit describes its latest build step.

Leave Check new descendant builds automatically after saving this setup selected to queue this check automatically, then choose Save test setup for this revision. For button sequences or a fixed comparison region, expand Advanced inputs and comparison region.
Create a build normally, or choose an existing Build to check and Run checks. The application shows progress and lets you cancel the job. It remains usable while separate workers run.
Open a recent result. Compare Original, Build and Difference. Read cartridge integrity, state replay and worker closure results alongside the visual result.

PASS means the configured checks passed. REVIEW means the image changed under the review policy. REGRESSION means an explicit assertion or integrity check failed. INCONCLUSIVE means the baseline was unstable, flat or otherwise unsuitable. BLOCKED explains why execution could not complete.

chapters.title: Find the ROM bytes behind a graphic
chapters.kicker: Verified graphic sources / step by step
chapters.intro: Go beyond matching pixels. ROMancer can recover source pixel origins with controlled builds, then test the recovered map independently. This workflow uses the tested literal tile formats across all six supported systems.
steps: Cold-start the game and reach the scene. Pause, capture a frame and save a tight sprite or tile trace. ROMancer records acknowledged inputs automatically.

In the saved trace choose Verify ROM sources. ROMancer replays the original twice, then runs coded probes and two independent validation patterns in temporary builds. Progress and Cancel job appear below.

Read the result. Verified visual source includes an exact file offset, a recovered pixel map and original/controlled-marker/difference pictures. Green mask pixels are verified; unresolved pixels stay red. A partial map does not certify the whole sprite.

Choose Open verified part in graphics editor. Its original source pixels and observed colors are shown. Make a small change, review it and create a separate build. Undo restores the editing stroke; the original ROM stays unchanged.

Saved source-test results retain earlier successful and unsuccessful pages. In Game view use Verified sources or Source checks to find the evidence again. Test next source locations continues a bounded search.
chapters.result: The supplied Castlevania test verified a graphic source at 0x1B167; the Rastan test verified one at 0x10400. Both were recovered and rechecked through ROMancer, then opened in its actual visual editor.
chapters.note: Offsets apply only to the tested revision and scene. This measures source-to-picture dependency, not CPU, mapper-bank or DMA transfers.

chapters.title: Edit a captured object as one connected picture
chapters.intro: Bring verified parts together instead of guessing how neighboring ROM tiles form a character. A saved layout keeps the captured placements, orientation, observed colors and shared-tile relationships.
steps: Reach a scene from a fresh cold start. Pause, select a tight region in Playtest, save its trace and choose Verify ROM sources. A whole object needs source verification for each selected part.

Under Whole object, select the verified placements that belong together. You can select parts from several saved result pages for the same trace and frame. Give the object a short name, then choose Open whole object.

The graphics editor shows the captured scene, source tiles and assembled editing preview. Select a source tile to highlight its captured placements. Empty cells stay empty, and recovered horizontal or vertical flips remain in the layout.

Paint in the assembled preview. If one stored tile appears in several places, the shared-use notice explains that all of those placements change together. Original and editing pictures, changed-pixel counts, stroke Undo and Redo remain available.

Expand Full-scene preview to compare the captured frame with the staged composite. The yellow outline marks the saved object. A changed-pixel count confirms the preview updated; the label says simulated because no new game frame has been run.
Review the edit, create a separate build and use Test this edit. Find the layout again in Saved objects or the Game view Saved objects category. Remove layout deletes only its metadata.
chapters.result: You edit a measured multi-part arrangement while keeping the scene and exact source uses visible. Object names describe your intent; ROMancer does not infer whether a captured object is a particular enemy or actor.
chapters.note: Only compatible aligned literal parts from the same authenticated trace, frame and execution setup can be combined. Overlaps, mixed codecs and ambiguous orientations are refused. A partial placement is clearly marked. Imported or historical layouts reopen as checked declarations, not fresh execution proof. Full-scene previews use captured colors at saved placements. Background behind transparency, priority, palette ownership, animation and other uses of the same bytes are not reconstructed. Old captures need a fresh trace to include the full frame.
chapters.caption: The actual Mossy Hollow hero source tiles and a staged one-pixel edit in its full captured scene. The yellow outline identifies the saved object.

chapters.title: Test an edit against the scene you captured
chapters.intro: Use your actual captured input history to check a separate build, with no custom test JSON. ROMancer checks that the original still reproduces the recorded scene before showing the edit comparison.
steps: Load the original from power on. Play to the scene, pause, then choose Save comparison scene. It uses a selected frame region when available. The default uses up to 256 × 256 pixels from the top left.

If you started with a sprite, choose Inspect graphics, drag around it and choose Find ROM source for selection. A saved graphics trace can also supply the comparison. Review the edit and create a build.
Choose Check my hack in the bottom bar. Under Compare a captured scene, choose the capture, then Test captured scene.
ROMancer checks that two runs of the original reproduce the saved frame, then compares the build using the same inputs. Review the original, build and difference pictures.
Look for the change you intended. REVIEW means pixels changed. INCONCLUSIVE means the comparison could not establish a stable baseline. BLOCKED shows the failed prerequisite.
chapters.result: The scene check is repeatable and tied to its exact source, descendant build and execution setup. It does not replace your saved automatic test policy.
chapters.note: This shortcut allows up to 2400 frames and 20 input steps. Longer or state-based scenarios belong in Routes and Regression. A different game revision, unrelated build, historical imported trace, battery-save start or changed core setup cannot silently reuse the capture.

details.title: Draft preview versus testing a saved build
details.text: Graphics & fonts can preview a staged draft before publishing a build. It requires a fresh trace from the exact original, a repeatable cold start, matching core/controller options and supported declared edits. The bound is 20 input steps, 2,400 frames, a 64 MiB source and 262,144 frame pixels. An unstable original yields Inconclusive and no edited picture. Record a shorter fresh capture or test a saved build instead. A changed frame is an observation, not proof of full-game correctness.

chapters.title: Check what should happen in gameplay
chapters.intro: Set a clear expectation for what should change in the game and what should stay the same. ROMancer runs the recorded input sequence twice on the original and once on your build.
steps: Open the original ROM. In Advanced, open Investigation. Under Memory watches, enter a name, region and offset, choose 1, 2 or 4 bytes, then select Add watch.
In Playtest, start from power on, play to the comparison point and choose Save comparison scene. Create a separate build from the original.
Select the build and open Check my hack. In Compare a captured scene, expand What should happen? and choose the saved watch.

Choose Final value for a raw number or Change during last input for the difference across the last recorded input step. Fill in the original and build numbers. For Same as original, leave those fields blank.
Add another check to verify a value that should stay the same. Choose Test captured scene and review the measured numbers and the three pictures.
chapters.result: In Mossy Hollow, 75 idle frames and 12 frames holding Right produced 24 pixels of movement in the original and 48 in the faster build. Health stayed at 5. Both gameplay checks passed.
chapters.note: When the original measurements disagree, the test is inconclusive. A stable result outside your expectations is a regression. The picture can still need review when all numeric checks pass.
chapters.caption: Actual ROMancer result for Mossy Hollow showing distance, health and a side-by-side scene comparison.

chapters.title: Try three verified practice edits
chapters.intro: Use the ROMs created by the included workshops. Each edit starts from its original, produces a separate build and has a reproducible gameplay comparison.
steps: Open Try the editing studio for Mossy Hollow. In Stats & data, set Hero speed from 2 to 4. Review and create a build. For the captured reference, wait 75 frames from power on and hold Right for 12 frames. The original moved 24 pixels and the build moved 48.
Select the original Mossy Hollow source again. In Text & layout, change HELLO, EXPLORER! to READY, EXPLORER! and create a separate text build. Compare the greeting at frame 90.

On the Overview start screen, open More practice ROMs and choose Game Boy Color workshop. In Graphics & fonts, choose palette entry 1 and set it to blue (#0000FF). Compare at frame 120. The red diamonds turn blue.
chapters.result: All three comparisons reproduced the original twice and showed the intended change in the new build. The three BPS examples independently reconstruct their respective builds.
chapters.note: Use Controller & frame tools in Playtest for exact counts. Set Frames to advance for a wait. Set Frames per input and click an arrow for a held direction.
chapters.caption: Actual original and edited emulator frames from the three practice projects.

chapters.title: Inspect bytes with useful context
steps: Open Advanced > Resources. Choose a documented location or enter a decimal or 0x hexadecimal offset and choose Go.

Read the file offset on the left, hex bytes in the middle and printable ASCII on the right. A centered dot stands for a nonprintable byte. The outline follows the selected byte in both columns. Underlined values are staged edits. Below the grid, Original and Draft show the exact selected byte.
Search AB ?? CD, UTF-8 or an integer with an explicit byte order. Open Number inspector & bookmarks to inspect or bookmark the selected offset.
Edit a byte using two hex digits. Use the footer Undo and Redo to check the staged change, then choose Review byte edits and Create separate build. Your original remains unchanged.
To share a build, open Export, select its Original ROM and Edited build, and create a verified patch. Keep the original ROM private.
chapters.result: The exact before/after byte change is reviewed, stored in a separate build and can be exported as an independently verified patch.
chapters.note: An uncatalogued ROM can use the same byte workflow when its cartridge layout is recognized. Before changing gameplay, find a checked definition or trace that connects the bytes to the intended behavior. The ASCII column shows standard characters. Custom game text may use a different encoding.
chapters.intro: Inspect exact stored bytes and create a separate reviewed build. Use a known location or higher-level editor when its definition describes the intended change.
chapters.caption: Original NES workshop. The staged byte and its ASCII character are underlined. The outline shows the selected pair.

details.title: Checksum policy · Advanced
details.text: Automatic checksum maintenance is the default. Under Advanced byte options, Preserve checksum fields explicitly requests byte-exact edits without repairing cartridge fields. Use it only when you understand the convention. A ROM whose stored checksum differs from the supported algorithm needs this explicit choice. A mismatch is reported; it is not silently repaired or certified. Changing policy requires a new review.

details.title: Name a confirmed byte
details.text: Use a controlled edit and a matching replay to check what a byte does. Select that byte on the original ROM, open Number inspector & bookmarks, enter a name and choose Preview named field. Stats & data opens the unsigned one-byte field. Save this layout makes it reusable for this exact source when no table layout is already saved.

chapters.image_alt: Selected hex byte and its ASCII character outlined, with the staged byte underlined

chapters.title: Trace a declared range to the exact bytes
chapters.intro: Follow a named table field, graphics resource or sound range into the selected source. Explanations show the encoding and meaning when a checked definition is available.
steps: In Resources, open Declared resource catalog, choose Index declared resources and search a name. Choose Inspect to open the bytes.

Select a byte in the hex editor. Open Number inspector & bookmarks, then Explain selected bytes. Read its source-bound name, offset, stored bytes, numeric value, byte order and declared bounds when available.
Use Declared resource relationships to follow related source ranges. Check the evidence for each relationship before using it to plan an edit.

In Advanced > Investigation, use Find declared references or Resolve address, then Inspect mapped bytes. Confirm the current source, mapping and bank. Recompute after switching sources; do not reuse a stale result.
chapters.result: The hex selection belongs to the intended artifact and declared file offset. The explanation identifies its bounded stored meaning, or explicitly reports that no interpretation has been established.
chapters.note: Use a checked declaration or runtime evidence before assigning gameplay meaning to stored bytes. Sound samples and known sequence fields each have their own scope.

details.title: What a declaration can explain
details.text: A table definition can identify the record, field, encoding and accepted range. Graphics and sound definitions identify the codec and storage bounds.

details.title: Use the matching kind of tool
details.text: A source editor changes checked stored data. A game-authoring engine needs its own executable runtime and event system. Instruction breakpoints require a real CPU-debugging adapter. The current investigation tools provide byte comparisons and bounded observations, not a full instruction debugger.

details.title: Protect the selected context
details.text: Reference jumps, mapped-address inspection and memory watches belong to a source/runtime context. Re-selecting a file, build or session requires a fresh compatible observation. A changed RAM value alone does not identify a ROM address or the instruction that wrote it.

chapters.title: Discover resources and declare a format
chapters.intro: Offline investigation can identify known revisions and suggest possible structures. A candidate is a lead to inspect, not permission to edit arbitrary bytes.
steps: Read the automatic investigation after import. Keep exact known identities separate from candidate text, graphics, pointer or compression matches.
Use Rescan ROM for changed data or Find resources for a focused byte range. Read any partial-range report and continue the next range when needed.
Confirm the offset, format, dimensions, allocation and source identity before declaring a resource. Inspect surrounding bytes and independent references for the exact revision.
Save the checked definition. Reopen it on the same source and compare the preview with a measured game scene before applying edits.
chapters.result: The editor decodes the intended resource from bounded, explicitly identified storage. A later build must meet the same source and original-byte preconditions.
chapters.note: A plausible picture or readable word can occur inside code or unrelated data. Automatic discovery cannot establish arbitrary enemy names, animation scripts or sound-driver commands.

details.title: System formats
details.text: NES stored CHR uses planar 2bpp; Game Boy uses paired row bitplanes. SNES templates support paired 4bpp; Genesis supports packed 4bpp and big-endian palette words. Each game can add compression and its own layout.

details.title: Six supported modes
details.text: NES, SNES, Genesis, GB, GBC and Master System are separate user choices. Bank switching, enhancement hardware and game-specific data need their own supported mapping or verified definition. Unrecognized cartridge layouts are rejected on import. Stored resource interpretations still need their supported codec and source-bound definition. A checked sound range can identify stored data for a supported sound format.

details.title: Automatic versus manual investigation
details.text: Settings enables Auto deep scan on ROM load by default. You can choose a manual scan instead. Automatic paused-gameplay graphics analysis examines available observed data; its candidates still need format and ownership confirmation.

chapters.title: Paint an assembled sprite
steps: Open Graphics & fonts. With verified or declared tiles loaded, use Sprite assembly to arrange the parts.

Click a brush color swatch, set Preview size to Fit or a fixed zoom, then paint in Editing · paint here. Declared, observed and unknown grayscale colors are labeled. The numeric Brush index remains available.
Use Undo sprite stroke or Redo sprite stroke, then Review graphics changes and create a build.
chapters.result: The capture shows an actual changed pixel on a 16 x 32 Simon assembly made from eight tiles.
chapters.note: This example uses a declared tile layout and observed gameplay colors. It does not prove automatic sprite assembly for every game. Preview colors do not change palette bytes. Compare changes in the viewing controls. Save edited PNG always exports the complete edited image, not a difference mask.
chapters.intro: An explicit assembly places known tiles into a useful sprite view. Painting edits the referenced tiles; the arrangement itself does not discover game logic.
chapters.caption: Actual ROMancer interface. The HTML edition links to the full-resolution capture.

chapters.title: Edit stored palette entries deliberately
chapters.intro: A pixel usually stores a color index. A palette supplies the RGB color for that index. Changing the palette can recolor many uses at once.
steps: Load declared graphics. If Preview colors > ROM palette bank appears, choose the bank used by the graphic. Tiles, assembled sprites and animation use it together. This selector changes the view only.
In Palette colors, select a bank and entry. Choosing an entry also selects its preview bank. Use Choose color or Color storage values; the edited views update while the original stays fixed.
Review the channel limits and shared consumers. RGB555 stores 5-bit channels, so a chosen screen color is quantized to a representable value.
Review graphics changes, create the build and inspect every scene known to share that palette. Verify the color in the actual game, not just the swatch.
chapters.result: The proposed color is representable in the declared format; the build changes the intended palette bytes and the scene uses them as expected.
chapters.note: Preview colors used to arrange a sprite are not necessarily stored palette edits. Transparency, banks and a game's dynamic palette changes can affect the observed result. A saved preview reopens only for matching source, schema, edits and trace evidence. Changing a pixel, map cell, palette or setup hides the older pictures. The separate object-placement composite is labeled simulated; it is not an emulated frame.

details.title: Shared entries
details.text: One stored entry may color many tiles, objects or frames. Preview-bank selection does not change pixels or palette bytes. Tilemap cells retain their encoded per-cell bank. Confirm shared consumers and compare an unchanged neighboring object.

details.title: Original versus edited
details.text: The original view remains the reference while the edited view follows staged values. Saving the editor draft does not modify the playable source. Build and reload before judging the in-game effect.

details.title: Native palette storage
details.text: Declared graphics palettes support Genesis RGB333, Master System RGB222 and RGB555 in either byte order. ROMancer decodes the channel bits and preserves unused bits. Game Boy monochrome uses four hardware shades. Missing palette evidence is labeled; index grayscale is not claimed as natural game color.

details.title: See the actual captured scene
details.text: For a declared palette or pixel edit, expand Preview this draft in a captured scene. Choose a cold-start capture and Preview captured scene. ROMancer replays the original twice and a temporary checked draft once with the captured inputs and core settings. Original replay, Draft replay and Difference are emulator frames. No build is added to your project until you choose Create graphics build.

chapters.title: Preview a draft in its actual captured scene
chapters.intro: See a palette or pixel change against the complete captured background before adding a project build. Choose a supported literal graphics format and a reproducible paused native scene.
steps: In Playtest, load the original from a fresh cold start. Advance to a useful scene, select a region under Inspect graphics and save a gameplay trace. A historical or state-loaded capture cannot establish a cold replay.
Open Graphics & fonts for that same original. Stage a declared palette or pixel change, then expand Preview this draft in a captured scene. Select the capture and choose Preview captured scene.

Compare Original replay, Draft replay and Difference. The original must reproduce twice. These are actual emulator frames from temporary checked copies; your paused session and project build history remain separate.

Return to another screen and reopen the editor: a validated matching preview returns. Change an edit and the old pictures disappear. Review and create the build to keep the result, then use Playtest saved build and Export saved build.
chapters.result: The previewed draft SHA-256 matched the separately created build in the six-system native checks. Use the native draft preview and compare its resulting frame before creating a build.
chapters.note: This check covers the captured inputs and settings. It does not establish every palette consumer, gameplay outcome or commercial sound engine. Object-placement composites remain explicitly simulated.

chapters.title: Preview an explicitly assembled animation
chapters.intro: Animation frames let you compare declared arrangements over time. They do not automatically identify or rewrite a commercial game's animation script.
steps: Arrange the tiles for one frame in Sprite assembly. Open Animation frames, set Frame duration (ms) and choose Add assembled frame.
Create the other explicit frame arrangements. Select a frame to inspect it, use Edit selected frame to revise its layout, or Remove selected frame to remove it from this preview.
Use Play animation and Pause animation to review the proposed sequence. Read the shared-tile count before changing pixels.
Review the actual asset changes and build them. Playtest the real game animation to establish whether its own script uses the edited tiles in the intended order.

Expand Save & reuse animation layouts. Name the arrangement, preview it, check its shared tiles, then save the reviewed layout. Up to 16 saved layouts are kept per source, each with 1–32 frames and 40–2,000 ms declared frame durations.

Use Load layout to reopen its exact graphics document and frame arrangements. Loading replaces the arrangement draft; tile edits stay separate. Saved layouts appear in Game view and are included in exported research packs. Delete saved layout removes that saved arrangement, not ROM bytes.
chapters.result: The preview cycles through the layouts you supplied and reflects staged tile/palette edits. The unchanged original remains available for comparison.
chapters.note: Editing a tile reused across frames changes every preview frame that references it. A timing value in this preview is not proof of the game's stored animation timing. Saved timing is author-declared. It does not rewrite the game’s animation table or prove which pose the engine will select. Edit a source tile to affect every frame using that tile, then build and playtest.

details.title: What is saved
details.text: The frame list is an explicit editor layout. Only supported reviewed asset changes become ROM bytes. Keep resource definitions and game-specific script evidence separate.

details.title: Useful first check
details.text: Make a one-pixel change in one tile, find every frame that shares it, then undo. This reveals the practical reach of a tile before you commit a larger redraw.

chapters.caption: Two original studio poses arranged, previewed and saved in the actual animation tools.

chapters.title: Paint a declared tilemap
chapters.intro: A tilemap is a grid of references to tiles. Entries can also contain palette banks or horizontal and vertical flip flags, depending on the declared format.
steps: Inspect a graphics definition that includes the tilemap location, dimensions, entry format and associated tile/palette resources. Confirm the original map preview.
Select the map brush or entry and stage the intended tile index, palette bank and flip values. Compare the map preview while keeping the original as the reference.
Use the tilemap editor's supported painting tools and undo controls for bounded strokes. For a specific entry, inspect its stored values before staging a change.
Review graphics changes and shared consumers. Create a build and load the game location that uses the map, including scrolling or transitions that might load other banks.
chapters.result: The reviewed map entry references a valid tile and allowed bank/flip values. The rendered game screen shows the intended arrangement.
chapters.note: A tilemap is a display arrangement. Collision, objects and exits can live in separate records and will not automatically follow a visual change.

details.title: PNG import
details.text: For supported graphics imports, choose exact palette mapping or explicitly review nearest-color conversion. Importing artwork does not establish the ROM's resource location or capacity.

details.title: Reuse matters
details.text: A tile edit changes every map entry that reuses that tile. A map-entry edit changes its reference instead. Pick the operation that matches the intended scope.

chapters.title: Rebalance named equipment and enemy stats
steps: In Overview > Game edits, open the desired attack, armor, helm, base-price or enemy-stat table. The original attack-only resource ID remains compatible with older definitions.
Search by name or ID, choose the record, and select Show selected record. Edit only the exposed numeric fields. The Original/Edited preview updates as you type.

Keep critical rates within 0 to 100. HP and prices use the declared integer widths; batch changes refuse numeric overflow and field-limit violations. Blank or unused slots are not promises of gameplay content.
Choose Review changes, inspect the exact records, then Create build. Playtest the new build. Stored attack, defense and prices can be transformed by game formulas or battle scripts.
chapters.result: A named record receives a checked fixed-width edit. The screenshot shows a real armor record and its changed defense preview.
chapters.note: The current definitions cover 85 weapon slots (74 named), 32 named armor slots, 24 named helms and 251 enemy slots (212 named). Effects, flags, rewards and scripts are preserved. These counts describe the exact original, not every external hack. For other games, table layouts still require a verified definition.
chapters.intro: The exact USA Chrono Trigger profile supplies named equipment and enemy tables. Names are decoded from your selected ROM, with record IDs kept beside duplicates and blank slots.
